newsitem.title: UK: Don't sell beliefs for power, British Liberals told.
newsitem.headline: Don't sell beliefs for power, British Liberals told.

text.p: Britain's Liberal Democrats declared on Thursday they were Britain's only party with principles, and cheered a party veteran who said they should not "sell out" for a share in government.
Shirley Williams was intervening in a controversy over whether the centrist minority party should be willing to join a coalition with Labour after the next election.
The question has dominated the party's annual conference, but Williams, a former Labour cabinet minister, said the answer depended on the policies to be pursued.

"Liberal Democrats must not be diverted from our key policy objectives. We must not exchange them for a handful of government posts," she told delegates on the final day of the conference. The election is due by May 1997.

Williams, who joined the Liberal Democrats in the 1980s, added: "It is our responsibility to hold any new government to them, to support it in achieving them, to remonstrate or even withdraw our support if it fails to attempt them."

The party's deputy leader attacked Labour, which will hold its last pre-election conference next week, saying it had been emasculated by a policy revolution under moderate, pragmatic leader Tony Blair.
"If Mr Blair took over from (Prime Minister John) Major in Downing Street tomorrow, remarkably little would change," deputy leader Alan Beith said in his keynote speech.
"Government without a firm basis of beliefs is a hopeless prospect. Such is the pressure of events that governments are driven this way and that, like sailing boats in a squall."
Blair has jettisoned most of Labour's traditional socialist policies, moving his party to the centre ground.

The shift prompted some senior party figures to suggest earlier this week that a coalition with Labour could be desirable after the election. The Liberal Democrats are now further to the left than Labour in some key policy areas.
Beith insisted only the Liberals now sought to help ordinary people, by daring to raise taxes to improve services such as education and health and by reforming Britain's unwritten constitution.

An opinion poll in Thursday's Times newspaper suggested Blair will not need allies in government, giving Labour a 23 point lead over the Conservatives, and the Liberals the support of just 14 percent of Britons.
But party leader Paddy Ashdown said Liberals need not be downhearted, pointing to successes in the past few years which have seen them outstrip the Conservatives in local government.

"We have set new standards in our town halls -- on open government, on good government, on environmental protection, crime prevention and education," he said. "We have made a difference. Now I want us to do the same nationally."

He said the party should not reveal its hand on cooperation with Labour before the election "There are many ways of exercising power and influence. Rule nothing in, rule nothing out, keep all options open, and campaign to win," he said.
In the 1992 election the Liberal Democrats won 17.8 percent of the vote but, under the country's first-past-the-post system, won only 20 seats in the 651-member parliament.
Party analysts say local government election trends suggest the party is close to a breakthrough in a series of seats they fell just short of winning in 1992.
